name: Kira Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so feel free to give me your public line and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the reconsiderations team at the regional benefits processing centre, the big grey building in the business park off the ring road. People who've been turned down for disability benefit ask us to look again, so my day is reading medical evidence, the original decision and whatever the claimant has sent in, then deciding if we got it wrong. I like the puzzle of it, and I like phoning someone to say the decision's changed. What wears me out is the evidence packs, some are two hundred pages of scanned letters.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much do AI tools come into that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I'm the digital champion for our floor, which means I test new tools and show people how to use them. I've written a set of prompts that summarise a medical pack into a one-page timeline, and about half the floor uses them now. I still read the key letters myself, because the summary misses things like a GP saying "on bad days".

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it out. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a little bit, because I always said these tools are helpers, not caseworkers. At work I'd keep running my lunchtime sessions on the summary prompts. Online I'd probably post something about how the hype cycle burned out, I follow a lot of that stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good news for me. I'm one of the people who gets the most out of the small gains, so I look quick and useful to managers. My pay's already at the top of the band for my grade and I've got almost a year of savings, so nothing here touches my money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for a team leader role on reconsiderations within a year. Being the person on the floor who knows the AI tools gives me an edge when the team leader job comes up. I'd keep improving the prompts so new starters can use them on day one. Jonas and I would carry on saving for a house without changing anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and maybe a bit disappointed. I like the tools, and part of me wanted to see what they could really do. But a steady job I'm good at is not a bad outcome.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in your work or life that worries you, even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The workload, really. Reconsiderations have doubled in two years because first decisions keep getting rushed. If AI doesn't speed things up, the pile just keeps growing, and I've seen good people on my floor burn out and leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a colleague who's never used the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say try the timeline prompt on one case and see if it saves you twenty minutes. That's how I got my colleague Dorota on board, she was sure it would be useless. Now Dorota sends me prompts she's improved.

say: I'd say these tools were always **helpers**, not caseworkers.
I'd post that the **hype cycle** finally burned out.
think: Small AI gains make me look **quick and useful**, which helps my career.
My pay and **year of savings** aren't touched at all.
do: Apply for a **team leader** role on reconsiderations within a year.
Keep improving the **summary prompts** for new starters.
feel: **Calm**, with a bit of **disappointment** that the tools stall.
S0.quote: Being the person on the floor who knows the AI tools gives me an edge when the team leader job comes up.
fieldNote: Kira sees AI as **career capital**, even when it stalls.
Her real pressure is a **doubling workload**, not technology.
She's slightly **disappointed** by the plateau, unusual for someone this exposed.

steps.text: Apply for a reconsiderations team leader post within a year
Rewrite the evidence summary prompts so new starters can use them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to redesign the work, not just bolt tools on. At work I'd be pushing to run the pilot, because I'd rather shape it than have it done to us. Online I'd be one of the people saying it's manageable if we plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the reading and summarising I do is exactly what goes first. But somebody has to check the AI's decisions and handle the cases it gets wrong, and I want to be that person. I think the team shrinks and I end up on the smaller team, running it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Within a month I'd ask to lead the reconsiderations pilot and write the checking process for AI decisions. I'd take an online course in data quality, about three hundred pounds, and pay for it myself if the centre won't. I'd keep saving as normal, because my savings are already solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly for other people. I feel fine about me. But I can picture the restructure meeting and the faces of people who never opened the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound sure you'd stay. What if you're wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I've got a year of savings and a skill everyone's hiring for. Every department will want someone who can check AI decisions. I'd be annoyed, but I'd find something within a few months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your floor would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My colleague Martin, who's fifty-five and still prints evidence packs to read on the bus. He's brilliant at spotting what a doctor really means, which the tools aren't. I'd fight to get him into the checking team, because his judgement is exactly what we'd need.

say: I'd say it's time to **redesign the work**, not just bolt tools on.
I'd say it's **manageable** if we plan.
think: The **reading and summarising** I do all day is the first thing to go.
I expect to land on the **smaller team**, checking AI decisions.
do: Ask to **lead the pilot** and write the checking process within a month.
Take a **£300 data quality** course, self-funded if needed.
S1.quote: Somebody has to check the AI's decisions and handle the cases it gets wrong, and I want to be that person.
fieldNote: Kira expects to **gain** from the change and plans to lead it.
Her unease is about **colleagues**, especially those who avoided the tools.
She values older colleague **Martin's judgement** over the software's.

steps.text: Volunteer to lead the reconsiderations AI pilot this month
Write the checking process for AI-made benefit decisions
Pay £300 for an online data quality course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say we need rules for AI decisions about people's money, fast, with a human who can be appealed to. At work I'd tell people to keep their heads and grab every bit of training. Online I'd be a lot less upbeat than usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this one scares me, because it beats my plan. If AI can do any thinking work as well as a person, it can check its own decisions too, and my edge is gone. And Jonas tests software for a living, so both our desk jobs go at about the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now, before 2028, I'd talk to Jonas about one of us moving towards hands-on work for the three-year gap. I'd look at occupational therapy assistant training, because it uses what I know about disability and it's physical. I'd pause the house plan and move some savings into something safer, and I'd volunteer for a disability charity to build contacts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the first time in this whole conversation I've felt the floor move. I'm usually the calm one, and here I'm not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said both your jobs go. What does that look like at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two people in their late twenties with no work and a good bank balance that shrinks every month. We'd have maybe two years of both savings together if we were careful. After that I genuinely don't know what the plan is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jonas that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not buying a house in 2027, and we're not going to pretend we know how this ends. Then probably we'd make a spreadsheet, because that's what we do when we're stressed. Jonas likes columns, I like timelines.

say: I'd demand rules giving every claimant a **human to appeal** to.
I'd tell colleagues to grab **every bit of training**.
think: AGI **beats my plan**, because it can check its own decisions.
Jonas tests software, so **both our desk jobs** go together.
do: Look into **occupational therapy assistant** training before 2028.
Pause the **house plan** and move savings somewhere safer.
Volunteer for a **disability charity** to build contacts.
feel: **Alarmed**, feeling the **floor move** for the first time.
S2.quote: If AI can do any thinking work as well as a person, it can check its own decisions too, and my edge is gone.
fieldNote: Kira's AI skills are her safety net, and this scenario **removes it**.
**Two desk incomes** in one household push her to alarmed.
She falls back on **hands-on care work** for the three-year robot gap.

steps.text: Research occupational therapy assistant courses before 2028
Volunteer at a local disability charity on weekends
Pause the 2027 house purchase with Jonas
Move some savings into a safer easy-access account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this well if governments start now. At work I'd push our centre to plan where every caseworker goes by 2031. Online I'd share what I'm learning, like I always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my AI edge buys me maybe three of those five years. After that the checking work goes too, unless the law says a person has to sign off. So I'd use the edge while it lasts and get ready for something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd lead the AI rollout at work and get the pay rise that comes with it. Then I'd start an occupational therapy degree part time, which is four years, and finish around 2031. Hands-on work gets until about 2034 here, and a therapist also has to talk to people, so it buys me more time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan, which makes a big difference to me. I like having a timeline. I'd still worry about Jonas, because testing goes earlier than therapy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is it strange to lead the rollout that ends your own job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Somebody's going to lead the AI rollout that ends my job, and I'd rather it was someone who cares about the claimants. And honestly, the extra pay funds the degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you and Jonas split the risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd agree that one of us moves to hands-on work early, and that's probably me, since I've got the disability knowledge. Jonas would stay in tech as long as it pays. We'd buy a small place in 2029 if things look stable, not before.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough if governments start now.
I'd push the centre to **plan a place** for every caseworker by 2031.
think: My AI edge buys me about **three years**.
After that, **checking work** goes too unless the law protects it.
do: **Lead the AI rollout** at work and take the pay rise.
Start a **part-time occupational therapy** degree, finishing around 2031.
feel: **Anxious**, but steadier because I have a **timeline**.
S3.quote: Somebody's going to lead the AI rollout that ends my job, and I'd rather it was someone who cares about the claimants.
fieldNote: Kira knowingly **leads the change** that will end her role.
She picks a **people-and-hands** career to stretch past 2034.
She and Jonas plan to **split the risk** between hands-on and tech.

steps.text: Lead the centre's AI rollout and take the higher grade
Start a four-year part-time occupational therapy degree
Delay buying a home with Jonas until 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to get this right, and I'd say it loudly. At work I'd want a ten-year plan for the whole centre. Online I'd be back to my usual hopeful self.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I come out of this fine. Ten years of being the AI person at work, then an occupational therapy career that runs to 2039 or beyond. I'd be thirty-seven when AGI lands, with a second career already started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd go for team leader and keep running the AI work. I'd start the therapy degree in year two or three, without rushing. Jonas and I would buy the house next year as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled, maybe a little uneasy. It's on my mind, but it doesn't keep me up. Ten years of warning makes AGI feel like a career change rather than a rescue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Therapy jobs might fill up with everyone else doing the same thing. Ten years is long enough for half my floor to have the same idea. So I'd watch the training numbers and switch to something else if it got crowded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything for Jonas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd nudge Jonas towards security testing, the side that checks whether AI systems are safe, because that might last longer. But it's Jonas's call. We'd sit down every year and see where we are.

say: I'd say ten years is a **real chance** to get this right.
I'd ask for a **ten-year plan** for the whole centre.
think: I'd be the **AI person** at work, then switch to therapy.
At **thirty-seven** I'd already have a second career started.
do: Start the **therapy degree** in year two or three.
Buy the **house** with Jonas next year as planned.
feel: Mostly settled, a little **uneasy**, like a **career change** rather than a rescue.
S4.quote: Ten years of warning makes AGI feel like a career change rather than a rescue.
fieldNote: Kira's mood eases sharply with **time to plan**.
She worries about **crowding** in therapy training, a sharp observation.
She keeps the **house plan** in this version only.

steps.text: Apply for team leader on the reconsiderations team this year
Enrol on an occupational therapy degree in year two or three
Buy a house with Jonas next year as planned

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it's the only one where my plan stops working and Jonas's job goes at the same time. What would help is a law that says a person must review any AI decision about someone's benefits. That keeps claimants safe and keeps some of us employed while we retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask who the claimants appeal to. In every one of these pictures, someone disabled is waiting for an answer about their rent and food. I'd want them to have a human to talk to, whatever happens to my job.

headlineQuote: In every one of these pictures, someone disabled is waiting for an answer about their rent and food.
portrait: Kira is a **27-year-old** caseworker on disability benefit reconsiderations at a regional processing centre.
She's her floor's **digital champion**, writing AI prompts that half her colleagues now use.
She stays calm or uneasy in the slower scenarios, expecting to **lead** the change.
AGI by 2028 alarms her because it **removes her AI edge** and hits partner Jonas's job too.
Her fallback is **occupational therapy**, which mixes her disability knowledge with hands-on work.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, where her plan fails and **both household jobs** go at once.
whatWouldHelp: A law requiring **human review** of every AI benefit decision.
